title: Coffee notes — inference papers + quick takeaways
text:
Quick brain dump after a few long coffees — high-level notes and actions from recent papers/blogs I read. Mostly for my own memory + to share with Maya/Omar when we sync. Not polished. 

Top themes I'm tracking
- KV/prefix caching: practical eviction policies, memory footprint, and cross-request prefix reuse. How much gain for real RLHF-style chats?
- Mixed-precision & quantization: where 4-bit/3-bit still safe, which layers to keep FP16 for quality-sensitive tokens.
- Batching/latency tradeoffs: continuous batching heuristics that don't explode p95.
- Lightweight evals: cheap shadow evaluation to catch hallucination regressions when swapping quantization or kernel sets.

Paper: "FlashKV++: adaptive prefix caching for long chat" (notes)
- Idea: hierarchical prefix index + hot-set detection per tenant, avoids cold-start cache pollution.
- Why interesting: aligns with our smart routing + per-tenant cache idea; could reduce token compute by 15-30% in workloads with long-lived sessions.
- Key methods: lightweight LRU with TTL boosted by request frequency, micro-profiling to detect reusable spans (not just token prefixes).
- Concerns: extra metadata + scan overhead on admission can increase tail latency if on critical path. Need async admission path.
- Experiment I'd run: simulate using recent Redwood chat traces (1 week, top 200 tenants) and compare hit-rate vs our current prefix-KV policy. Measure cost savings and extra CPU for metadata.

Paper: "QuantDyn: dynamic per-layer quantization based on token-sensitivity"
- Idea: compute a cheap sensitivity score per token or per position using a tiny probe network, then pick per-layer bitwidth for that invocation.
- Practicality: sounds expensive unless probe is tiny and cached across similar prompts. If we can amortize for multi-turn, maybe worth.
- Risk: complexity in runtime could cause jitter; harder to certify for enterprise customers.
- Quick take: prototype on one small model (7B) offline to see gains on perplexity and generation quality. If delta >10% compute reduction for <1% quality drop, it's promising.

Blog: "Batching heuristics that don't wreck tail latency (engineering notes)"
- Three heuristics I liked: time-fence with priority bypass, continuous micro-batching, and dynamic backpressure that learns per-model optimal window.
- Implementation note: our serving runtime already has adaptive batching hooks, but we don't expose per-customer priority lanes. Consider adding a cheap priority token in request header.
- To-do: add a small canary that gives 1% of traffic priority bypass and measure p95.

Conference takeaway: NeurIPS workshop on evals + quality monitoring
- Recurring theme: unit tests for quality (prompt sets + reference assertions) are now table stakes. People combine shallow automated checks with human-in-the-loop periodic drift evaluation.
- Good idea: shadow-eval pipeline that runs on a sample of real requests and computes a small set of metrics (factuality score, hallucination probe, toxicity). Keep retention 30 days.
- How this maps to Redwood Optimize: we can add a lightweight shadow-eval stage tied to rollout policy. If model fails metrics, auto-fallback to previous version.

Notes-to-self: short checklist for next sprint
- [ ] Run prefix-KV admission simulation on redwood-chat-traces (data request from infra) — estimate delta in token-level compute and p95 latency impact. (owner: me)
- [ ] Prototype tiny probe network for QuantDyn on 7B quantized model (owner: Omar)
- [ ] Add priority-bypass canary to adaptive batching (owner: Maya)
- [ ] Draft design doc for shadow-eval integration into rollouts (owner: me)

Open questions / things that bug me
- Are we measuring hit quality change for cached prefixes? Caching can bias outputs if we reuse old KV states for slightly different prompts. Need a metric for "cache-induced drift".
- How often do we need to refresh sensitivity probes for quantization? Every model update probably invalidates them. Can we amortize across minor checkpoints?
- Runtime complexity: adding per-request adaptivity (dynamic quantize, admission checks) increases code paths that SRE must debug. Operational cost vs compute cost tradeoff needs a spreadsheet.

Useful links I kept in the article margins
- benchmark script sketch: scripts/kv-cache-sim/README.md (on local repo)
- quick perf numbers: 7B fp16 baseline: 35ms/context-step p50, 105ms p95 on A100-80GB (our infra numbers from Sep run)

Short summaries of 3 quick papers (one-liners):
- Paper A: adaptive prefix indexes give ~20% compute reduction for chat workloads with heavy prefix reuse. (good for dedicated customers with long sessions)
- Paper B: per-layer dynamic quantization can save 30% compute if probe is cheap; riskier for latency SLOs.
- Paper C: learned batching windows reduce p95 by giving up some throughput; nice when SLOs matter more than cost.

If I get time before Friday
- spin up a small experiment for cache hit quality: replay 10k sessions and compare outputs with and without cache (same random seed). Flag cases where token probability distributions diverge > threshold.
- write a short Confluence page summarizing the acceptance criteria for introducing adaptive quantization in our runtime.

Random thought: could we use a cheap vector signature of the last N tokens to decide whether cached KV is safe to reuse? Something like a Bloom-filter-like fingerprint — cheaper than full semantic compare. Worth prototyping.

End of dump. Will tidy and turn into a proper PRD if any of the experiments look promising.

-- Evan
